newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE-Singapore electoral change stirs debate.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Singapore electoral change stirs debate.

text.p: Multi-ethnic Singapore, highly sensitive to racial issues since bloody riots over three decades ago, is locked in a quiet debate over whether proposed electoral changes could weaken the voice of minorities in parliament.

Sections of the public and some academics have argued that the move to raise the number of members of parliament who can be elected in multi-member group representation constituencies (GRCs) could reduce minority ethnic representation.
General elections are due in Singapore by April 1997.

"With the proposed amendment, instead of strengthening the protection (of minority representation), it would weaken it," lawyer Shriniwas Rai wrote in the Straits Times newspaper. The proportion of minority MPs would fall if the number in each GRC was limited to one, he said.

Singapore's minorities include Malays at 14.1 percent of the population, Indians at 7.1 percent, and other races -- which include a mix of Eurasians and Arabs -- at 1.1 percent. Chinese form the majority of Singapore's three million people.

Due to its multi-ethnic mix, Singapore handles the issue of race, language and religion with extreme sensitivity. The government frowns on Singaporeans criticising each others' race, culture and language and forbids religious missionaries from actively trying to convert people.

To prevent the build-up of racial enclaves, the government in 1989 introduced a policy which caps the number of residents from certain ethnic groups living in the same block in public housing estates.
This had raised concerns that a candidate from a minority group might find it hard to win a seat in parliament if Singaporeans decided to vote along ethnic lines in future elections.

However, the government amended the constitution in 1988 to create GRCs so that minority communities would always be represented in parliament. At its inception, there was a maximum of three MPs in a GRC. That was raised to four in 1991.
In the GRCs, votes are cast for slates rather than single candidates. The team winning the most votes takes all the seats. Each team must include at least one minority member.

The fresh concerns over minority representation stem from two bills tabled by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong early this month to increase the maximum number of MPs who can be elected from GRCs to six from four.
The proposed changes would also permit a reduction of single member wards to eight from the current 21. There are now 15 GRCs from a total of 81 seats, with 17 minority MPs in GRCs.
Goh's changes could in theory cut the number of GRCs to 12 or 13, and thus the number of guaranteed minority seats.

Goh has said the proposed increase in MPs per GRC was to allow for better management of town councils, which run public housing estates, and to create community development councils to promote social bonding. Parliament will debate the changes on October 28.
But Rai said if Goh wanted bigger town councils, he could propose two GRCs to form one council.
Constitutional lawyer Kevin Tan said the proposed changes deviate from the original objectives which led the government to amend the constitution in 1988.

"If the original purpose was to ensure minority representation, you should tamper with the constitution only for this purpose and not to hijack it for all other purposes," Tan told Reuters. "You are asking the institution of GRC to do more than what it's supposed to do."

Goh has told Singapore media his ruling People's Action Party (PAP) will field more than one minority candidate in a GRC which has six MPs if there is a danger of minority representation being reduced. He said there was also the possibility that not all GRCs would have six MPs.

But he said that while it was a good idea to state in the constitution that all GRCs should have at least two minority candidates, this could only be done in 10 years to better reflect Singapore's multiracial nature.
"We don't want to have one community which dominates the others purely because its numbers are bigger," Goh said.

Political scientist Shee Poon Kim said if minority groups felt strongly about political representation, it would be better to state in the constitution now that each GRC should have at least two minority MPs, than to have to wait.
"This will give them (the minorities) a sense of psychological security," he said.
